detail: catalytic (Ni) decomposition
description: catalytic decomposition (cracking) of methane, CH4 -> C + 2H2, over supported Ni (also Co, Fe or carbon) catalysts, producing CO/CO2-free hydrogen and solid filamentous carbon; the catalyst is regenerated by steam gasification or air oxidation of the carbon. Continuous operation needs twin fluidised beds (cracking and regeneration)

description: steam Rankine cycle: waste heat boiler raising steam for a condensing steam turbine; the most common WHP system in the US and the most familiar to industry

detail: Kalina cycle (ammonia-water)
description: Kalina cycle: Rankine cycle on an ammonia-water mixture; 15-25% more efficient than an ORC at the same temperature and highest theoretical efficiency, but complex, so suited to systems of several MW or more

detail: organic Rankine cycle
description: organic Rankine cycle: an organic working fluid with a lower boiling point than water drives a turbine on waste heat; can be sized economically in sub-MW packages and run with air-cooled condensers and unattended

basic oxygen converter: oxygen is blown onto hot metal to burn out carbon, with inert gas (typically argon) injected at the bottom to stir melt and slag, which lowers iron losses and phosphorus content

blast furnace producing liquid hot metal (pig iron) by smelting sinter or pellets in a reducing environment, with coke acting as both reducing agent and fuel and oxygen-enriched air blown in at the bottom

oxygen blast furnace: pure oxygen replaces oxygen-enriched air and part of the blast furnace gas is recycled, the recycle stream split into a cold flow injected at the bottom and a hot flow injected higher up; combined with capture on the top gas

plasma-heated blast furnace: part of the top gas is fed to a plasma burner, the CO2 in it converted back to CO by endothermic reaction with carbon from coke; needs neither hot blast, oxygen nor additional auxiliary reductants
blast furnace with pulverised coal injection and top gas recycling, with CO2 capture and storage on the top gas
coke oven: coal pyrolysis in an oxidation-free atmosphere. Air cannot be used because the oxygen would ignite the hot coke; the coke is quenched with water or with inert gas at the end of the grate

electric arc furnace melting ferrous scrap, increasingly with direct reduced iron in the charge; scrap is pre-heated by the furnace's own off-gases and charged with lime or dolomitic lime as a slag flux, and oxygen lances or oxy-fuel burners may assist the early melting stages

pellet plant: iron ore is converted into 9-16 mm balls while its iron content is upgraded, in four steps - grinding and drying, green ball preparation, induration, and screening and handling. Induration transforms almost all magnetite into hematite, which is why the process needs a large amount of heat. Mostly used at mining sites
HYL / Energiron direct reduction, natural-gas based; the brief calls it Hylsa

MIDREX direct reduction: pellets or lump ore descend a shaft furnace against a counter-flowing reduction gas enriched in hydrogen and carbon monoxide, reformed from natural gas; four stages - reduction gas, reforming, heat recovery and briquette making

sinter plant: ores, additives, recycled sinter and coke breeze are blended in a mixing drum, loaded onto a moving grate and ignited, with air drawn down through the bed by fans so the combustion front travels downwards; the sinter is cooled separately and crushed. Mostly used at integrated steelworks
COREX smelting reduction with CO2 capture and storage

COREX smelting reduction: iron ore is pre-reduced in a solid-state shaft, then smelted and further reduced in a vessel where coal is gasified with oxygen, delivering heat and a CO-rich gas that is returned to the pre-reduction shaft; uses coal directly, so no coking is needed
Hismelt smelting reduction, fed with iron ore fines and coal fines. Costs exclude iron ore fines, coal fines, oxygen gas, flux lime, natural gas and electricity consumption (p.4).

detail: with cogeneration
description: Tecnored smelting reduction, with cogeneration. Costs exclude coke, pellets, lime, natural gas and electricity consumption (p.4).

detail: without cogeneration
description: Tecnored smelting reduction, without cogeneration. Costs exclude coke, pellets, lime, natural gas and electricity consumption (p.4).

CALIX process: rapid calcination of dolomite in superheated steam in a reactor, with a residence time of seconds to inhibit sintering and phase separation, followed by rapid quenching. CO2 from the flash calciner is captured by a separate scrubbing system in which waste heat decomposes mineral sorbents, the sorbents re-carbonate against cold flue gas and are recycled

modern reciprocating (3rd generation) grate clinker cooler, introduced in 1983. Cooling air is recirculated to the preheater kiln as secondary air or to the precalciner as tertiary air; exhaust from the aftercooling zone is used for drying raw materials, mineral additives or coal. It replaced the travelling (2nd generation) grate cooler on heat recovery, and it is preferred to rotary and planetary coolers - planetary coolers cannot be used with precalciner kilns because tertiary air cannot be extracted from them
high pressure grinding rolls for cement grinding, the state-of-the-art choice where mineral additions are limited
vertical roller mill for cement grinding, the state-of-the-art choice where mineral additions are high
cement clinker kiln as measured across the existing EU fleet - the population Table 7's environmental block reports on, not any one of the kiln types above

dry process rotary kiln with a multistage (4-6) cyclone preheater and a precalciner - the brief's state-of-the-art technology for new dry plants. The precalciner is a secondary combustion chamber between preheater and rotary kiln where some 65% of total fuel is burnt and 60-65% of total kiln emissions are released; calcination is at least 90% complete before the raw meal reaches the rotary kiln
fluidised bed cement kiln - an emerging technique. Two Japanese pilot plants of 20 t/d and 200 t/d have run since 1989 and 1996; a 1000 t/d pilot kiln is under construction in China
Lepol kiln for semi-dry and semi-wet processes, with a travelling grate preheater installed outside the rotary kiln
long dry rotary kiln with no preheater

dry process kiln with a 5-stage preheater and precalciner and oxy-combustion capture. CO2 is captured ONLY from the precalciner - not from the kiln, the cooler or the raw mill - which is why its abatement is roughly two thirds of the post-combustion route's at 60% of the capital cost. Available for new kilns only; it cannot be retrofitted

dry process kiln with a 5-stage preheater and precalciner and post-combustion CO2 capture. Chemical absorption is the most appropriate of the post-combustion routes; membranes and carbonate looping are longer-term candidates. Applicable both to new kilns and as a retrofit to existing ones
dry process rotary kiln with a 1-4 stage cyclone preheater and NO precalciner

semi-wet route in which a filter cake is dried to a raw meal in an external drier and loaded into a 3-4 stage suspension preheater and precalciner kiln; the brief says this system offers both the lowest heat consumption and the highest clinker capacity of the semi-wet options
wet process route in which the slurry is first dried in an integral dryer crusher and then fed to a 2-stage precalciner kiln; the modern replacement for the long wet rotary kiln
long wet rotary kiln with an internal drying and preheating system

ZEOBOND geopolymer cement: fly ash and bottom ash from power stations, blast furnace slag and concrete waste activated with sodium and potassium hydroxide to make an alkali-activated cement. Needs no calcination of calcium carbonate and no high-temperature kiln, and would need less capital investment than a conventional plant

combined-cycle CHP: gas turbine with HRSG driving a steam turbine with back-pressure (all exhaust steam to process) or controlled extraction (pass-out, remainder condensed); favoured in process industry for its higher electrical efficiency, 20 up to hundreds of MWe. Minimum electric efficiency about 40% with full steam use; above 57% in condensing mode

gas turbine with heat-recovery steam generator (GT-HRSG): turbine exhaust raises high- or low-pressure steam or hot water in the HRSG; cost-effective for a few MWe up to 25 MWe; performs best at full power; heat can also drive absorption chillers

detail: landfill-gas engines
description: gas-engine CHP units on landfill gas (Table 2): 800 kWe at 1200 rpm, 1.2 bar fuel pressure, exhaust 465 degC before heat recovery, heat rate 9.76 MJ/kWh; 3000 kWe at 900 rpm, 4 bar, exhaust 365 degC, heat rate 9.04 MJ/kWh (LHV, full load)
gas-engine CHP unit on natural gas (Table 2, 68 kWe): engine speed 1500 rpm, fuel pressure 1.2 bar, exhaust gas temperature not given (N/A), electric heat rate ~10.5 MJ/kWh (LHV, full load)

gas-fired internal combustion engine generator with heat recovery from exhaust gas and cooling water, from kWe to a few MWe; natural gas or landfill gas. Without abatement NOx is 700-2000 g/MWh; with SCR 135-700 g/MWh

detail: fluidised-bed boiler with back-pressure or extraction turbine; capex per condensing-mode kWe
description: fluidised-bed combustion (FBC) boiler with steam turbine for industrial steam or district heating, firing coal, lignite or solid biomass (bark, sawdust, wood chips, residues) or several fuels co-fired; bed temperature 780-900 degC; CFBC units up to 475 MWe (Lagisza). The brief does not say whether the turbine is back-pressure or extraction - p.2 allows either

detail: digester plus engine; the cost includes the digester
description: anaerobic digestion of wet biomass (manure, co-digested agricultural residues) to biogas burnt in an internal-combustion gas engine for CHP; tens of kWe up to a few MWe

detail: biomass steam CHP
description: solid-biomass CHP or power plant: boiler (water-cooled vibrating grate VG, bubbling fluidised bed BFBC or circulating fluidised bed CFBC) raising steam for a steam turbine, on wood residues, forestry residues, waste wood or straw. From a few MWe to 350 MWe; plants of 7-20 MWe are used for CHP (Germany), 50-65 MWe for power only (UK); optimal CHP size about 20 MWe given a < 50 km sourcing area

detail: heat plant, mainly district heating; typical 100 MWth
description: geothermal heating plant: high- or low-enthalpy geothermal fluid used directly for heat - district heating (the most common use), space heating and cooling, industry, greenhouses, fish farming, spas. Site-sensitive because steam and hot water cannot be carried far

binary-cycle geothermal power plant: low- or medium-enthalpy resource fluid heats a process fluid in a closed loop through heat exchangers (organic Rankine or Kalina cycle); the exhaust resource fluid is re-injected with all its original constituents, so the plant is zero-discharge

detail: four US plants of 10-40 MWe as cases
description: four conventional binary-cycle geothermal power plants in operation or to be built in the US, 10-40 MWe

detail: low-pressure O2 for oxy-fuel and pre-combustion capture, 3000 t/d
description: cryogenic air separation producing low-pressure oxygen at large scale, for oxyfuel and pre-combustion capture (a 250 MW IGCC needs about 2000 t O2/day)

detail: iron-and-steel sector abatement cost; TGR-BF named as the technology of choice
description: CO2 capture in iron and steel making; the technology of choice is a new-design blast furnace with oxygen injection, top-gas recycling and CO2 removal by physical solvents (the brief says 'physical adsorbents'); chemical absorption is the alternative

detail: refinery flue gas; regeneration heat from natural gas
description: post-combustion CO2 capture at UK refineries, with the capture energy supplied by natural gas; reformers, catalytic crackers and vacuum distillation account for 30-40% of refinery energy use

detail: sector abatement cost ($/t avoided), incl. compression and re-injection
description: separation of CO2 from natural gas to meet pipeline specification (about 2% CO2) by chemical solvents (alkanolamines, MEA, DEA) at low CO2 concentration, or membranes at high concentration, with compression and re-injection into nearby formations (Sleipner, Snohvit, In-Salah)

detail: sector abatement cost; regeneration steam 1.5 GJ/t clinker
description: back-end chemical absorption of CO2 from the cement kiln off-gas (25-35% CO2); oxyfuel kilns and calcium looping are the alternatives the brief names without figures
onshore/offshore pipeline transport of dehydrated supercritical CO2 over 100 km; shipping is for small quantities (shipping row in the sidecar)
pipeline transport of supercritical CO2 (density about ten times natural gas); pumping stations about every 200 km vs 120-160 km for natural gas
CO2 pipeline construction; costs depend on location (up to 15 times higher in populated areas than remote regions) and operating pressure; steel prices doubled 2003-mid-2008

detail: sector abatement cost
description: capture of the high-purity CO2 that ammonia plants already separate from hydrogen by solvent absorption; part is used for urea (0.9 tCO2/t urea), the rest (about 180 MtCO2/yr globally) is vented
injection and storage of CO2 in deep (>800 m) saline formations, onshore or offshore
geological storage of CO2 - wells, compression and injection, operation and monitoring - in saline formations and depleted oil and gas fields; offshore wells cost several times onshore

process: Storage in oil and gas fields with enhanced recovery (p.5 text)
detail: storage with enhanced oil recovery
description: CO2 injection for enhanced oil recovery with storage (oil density < 910 kg/m3, depth > 600 m); 0.1-0.5 t oil per t CO2 injected

detail: utility peaking OCGT, 10-300 MWe
description: open-cycle (simple-cycle) gas turbine: air compressor and gas turbine on one shaft driving a generator; almost two-thirds of the turbine's gross output drives the compressor. Used for peak-load service. Aero-derivative units reach 41-42% but are limited to 40-50 MWe; heavy-duty units burn heavier fuels more readily

process: Bitumen upgrading to synthetic crude oil (text)
description: Upgrading of bitumen to a lighter synthetic crude oil by raising the hydrogen-to-carbon ratio, either by removing carbon (coking) or adding hydrogen (hydrocracking)

process: Oil sand surface mining with hot-water extraction (text)
detail: surface mining and extraction together; only the ore-to-bitumen ratio is given
description: Surface mining of oil sand within about 75 m of the surface: oil sand is shovelled by large machines and hauled to an extraction plant, where bitumen is separated from the sand with hot water and chemicals; about 90% of the bitumen is recovered. The bitumen is sold raw or upgraded to synthetic crude oil

process: Cyclic steam stimulation (CSS) thermal in-situ recovery, Canadian oil sands (text)
description: Cyclic steam stimulation: steam is injected into vertical wells to heat the bitumen, which is then pumped to the surface through the same well; recovery about 25-30% of the bitumen. TRAP: the brief writes 'CCS' for cyclic steam stimulation (CSS) throughout the oil-sand text ('two large CCS facilities', 'SOR ... 3.4 for CCS', 'about 70% against 25%-30% from CCS') and misnames it 'Cycle Steam Simulator' - it is NOT carbon capture and storage.

process: SAGD thermal in-situ recovery, Canadian oil sands (text)
description: Steam-assisted gravity drainage: two horizontal wells; steam injected in the upper well heats the bitumen, which drains to and is produced from the lower well. Needs thick, clean deposits; uses less energy and recovers more bitumen (about 70%) than cyclic steam stimulation. Steam raised mostly from natural gas in Canada

Oxygen-blown British Gas/Lurgi (BGL) slagging moving-bed gasifier plant producing syngas, no CO2 capture; commercial-size design from NETL-401 (2007), identical design run on two coals (cases: Illinois No. 6 bituminous and Wyodak Powder River Basin sub-bituminous)

process: Coal gasification system, BGL fixed-bed (summary table)
description: Coal gasification to syngas: oxygen-blown fixed-bed BGL gasifier with air separation unit, Rectisol acid gas removal and sulphuric acid plant; summary values spanning bituminous and sub-bituminous coal. Table 2 system: ASU, oxygen-blown fixed-bed BGL 1000 gasifier, acid gas removal (Rectisol), sulphuric acid plant

process: Coal gasification system, BGL fixed-bed (summary table)
detail: syngas with hydrogen separated by PSA
description: Coal gasification to syngas with co-production of hydrogen (about 20% of output) separated by pressure swing adsorption; same BGL/ASU/Rectisol/sulphuric-acid system as the syngas column. p.4: 'only slightly more costly' - 5% higher capital and 4% higher product cost than the basic process

process: Coal gasification system, BGL fixed-bed (summary table)
description: Coal gasification to synthetic natural gas (pipeline-quality SNG): the BGL/ASU/Rectisol system plus water gas shift reactor and methanation reactor. p.4: capital cost about 25% and production cost 40% higher than syngas, conversion efficiency over 14 percentage points lower

indirect coal-to-liquids: ASU, oxygen-blown entrained gasifier, shift converter, Fischer-Tropsch reactor and product upgrading, with power generation and CO2 separation; input coal, water, air; three sizes (10,000, 30,000 and 60,000 bbl/d)

process: NETL commercial-scale Fischer-Tropsch plant, Illinois No. 6 coal (Table 1)
detail: NETL plant with on-site power and CO2 capture (32,481 t/d)
description: indirect coal liquefaction: oxygen-blown gasification of Illinois No. 6 bituminous coal, gas clean-up, Fischer-Tropsch synthesis and product upgrading to naphtha and diesel, with on-site power generation and CO2 capture (32,481 t/d captured); NETL baseline assessment DOE/NETL-2007/1260
gas-to-liquids: ASU, steam reformer, shift converter, Fischer-Tropsch reactor and product upgrading (CO2 separation); input natural gas; three sizes (10,000, 30,000 and 60,000 bbl/d)

detail: driver not stated
description: Compressor stations installed every 65-160 km along onshore natural gas pipelines to restore the pressure lost to friction; the driver runs on the transported gas itself or on electricity (the brief does not say which the cost and energy figures refer to)

detail: whole base-load LNG plant incl. pretreatment and NGL recovery
description: Base-load LNG liquefaction plant: removes impurities (S, CO2, H2O, O2) and recovers natural gas liquids, then cools and liquefies the gas at -162 degC in a refrigerant cycle whose compressors are usually driven by gas turbines fired on natural gas. The most expensive link of the LNG chain (30-45% of chain cost)

detail: driver not stated (electric, diesel or gas turbine)
description: Pump stations located every 32-160 km along onshore crude oil and product pipelines, keeping the oil flowing at 1-6 m/s; pumps driven by electric motors, diesel engines or gas turbines. Pumping need rises in cold climates because oil viscosity rises
cast house: molten aluminium is degassed and cast into ingot or billet
Bayer process alumina refinery: bauxite ore is ground, mixed and digested to extract aluminium oxide. Most primary aluminium smelters do not have alumina production on site

inert (carbon-free) anode cell. With the anode no longer consumed there is no anode carbon to oxidise, which removes the 1.6-1.9 t CO2/t of anode emissions entirely. The brief pairs it with wettable cathode materials as the two emerging routes to a more efficient electrolysis
Prebaked electrolytic cell WITHOUT flue gas scrubbing - the same cell as the Prebake entry above, kept separate because Table 1 gives it its own emissions column and the difference is large

centre worked Prebaked (CWPB) electrolytic cell with automatic multiple point feeding of alumina - the brief's best available technique for primary aluminium. Anodes are baked in a separate plant and consumed in the bath; a high current of 200-350 kA passes through the electrolyte at about 960 degC. A smelter is many cells in series, a pot-line. Flue gases go to a scrubber

modernised Soderberg cell: point feeders, improved burners, dry anode paste and better anode casing and cover, with a scrubber. p.3 credits the package with a 15% improvement in current efficiency and better environmental performance

Vertical Stud Soderberg (VSS) cell with a scrubber - the oldest configuration in Table 1 and the most expensive to convert: p.3 singles out the VSS-to-point-feeder-Prebake conversion as the one upgrade requiring major technical changes, at 2500-4000 EUR/t against 100-1000 EUR/t for every other route

Soderberg electrolytic cell, in which the anode paste is baked in place by the heat of the cell rather than in a separate anode plant. Less efficient and more polluting than Prebake, and the brief expects these plants to be closed or converted
secondary aluminium: scrap metal remelted in a furnace. Energy use can be cut further with enclosures or hoods over the feeding and tapping areas, and possibly heat recovery
prebaked carbon anode plant: petroleum coke and pitch formed into anodes and baked in a separate furnace before going to the cells

detail: dish-Stirling: 750 degC is the receiver/engine temperature, not delivered process heat (kept with this warning, modeller 2026-09-25)
dish-Stirling: 750 degC is the receiver/engine temperature, not delivered process heat (kept with this warning, modeller 2026-09-25)
description: solar dish: parabolic dish with two-axis tracking focuses sunlight (concentration above 1,300 in Table 1) on a receiver at the focal point driving a Stirling engine or micro-turbine; modular 5-50 kW (Table 1 0.025 MW); no cooling water needed

detail: field of a CSP power plant
field of a CSP power plant
description: linear Fresnel reflector: rows of ground-level flat or slightly curved mirrors with single-axis tracking focus on a fixed receiver tube several metres above, often with a secondary mirror; water is evaporated directly to saturated steam (direct steam generation); cheaper mirrors but lower optical efficiency than trough; thermal storage harder with direct steam generation

detail: field of a CSP power plant
field of a CSP power plant
description: parabolic trough: single-axis tracking parabolic mirrors (arrays up to 100 m long, 5-6 m aperture) concentrate sunlight 60-80 times on an evacuated receiver tube on the focal line; synthetic oil (to 390 degC), steam or molten salt (to 550 degC) carries the heat to a steam generator; more than 90% of installed CSP

detail: field of a CSP power plant
field of a CSP power plant
description: solar tower: two-axis heliostats concentrate sunlight (concentration 600-1,000) on a receiver on a central tower; heat-transfer fluid water-steam (250-300 degC), synthetic oil (390 degC), molten salt (565 degC) or gas (above 800 degC); molten salt allows cheap high-temperature storage (Gemasolar, 15 h)
centrifugal chiller - among the most efficient heat pump devices in the brief. Combined with thermal storage it cuts peak power; inverters cut consumption at low load

electrically driven vapour-compression heat pump on the reverse Carnot cycle: an evaporator takes heat from a low-temperature source, a compressor raises the fluid's temperature, a condenser releases the heat at the sink, and an expansion valve restarts the cycle. Sources include outdoor air, river, lake and sea water, ground heat, industrial and residential waste heat, and sewage heat. In industrial use it replaces boilers in many processes
industrial heat pump delivering heat directly rather than through steam - hot air for drying and similar low-temperature process duty
industrial heat pump raising steam into the medium-temperature band, up to 165 degC

molten carbonate fuel cell: lithium-potassium carbonate electrolyte molten at about 650 degC; direct internal reforming and no expensive catalyst; low power density needs large cell area; CO2 must be recirculated from exhaust to cathode; must be kept hot even on standby; stacks last about 5 years and can be replaced in the existing balance of plant; leads the large stationary market (arrays of tens of MW)

detail: electrical efficiency more than 15% below SOFC and MCFC; a candidate for its own archetype
description: phosphoric acid fuel cell: phosphoric acid electrolyte in a silicon carbide matrix; stack needs hydrogen so a fuel reformer and gas-shift stage are in the balance of plant; platinum is 10-15% of system cost; low power density suits large CHP installations; long commercial history; delivers low-grade heat

solid oxide fuel cell: ceramic electrolyte conducting oxide ions at 500-700 degC (intermediate-temperature varieties) or 850-1000 degC (regular); direct internal reforming lets methane feed the stack with little fuel processing; high operating temperature gives high-grade heat for industrial process heat, steam or hot water, and combined-cycle use; main challenge is stack degradation and thermal-cycling stress

detail: phase-change storage
description: latent heat storage in phase change materials (PCM): heat stored in a solid/liquid (or solid/solid) phase change at a fixed temperature, giving a constant discharge temperature and about 100 kWh/m3 (e.g. ice) against about 25 kWh/m3 for sensible storage; materials from ice (0 degC) and paraffins (-5 to 120 degC) to salt hydrates and sugar alcohols (erythritol 118 degC); industrial R&D targets high-temperature PCM above 150 degC

detail: phase-change storage
sensible storage
description: sensible heat storage: a liquid or solid medium (water, sand, rocks, concrete, molten salt) heated or cooled and kept in an insulated tank or underground; water tanks up to 80-90 degC charging, oil or molten salt above 100 degC (salt to 550 degC), ceramics and concrete for very high temperatures; cheapest TES but low energy density (about 25 kWh/m3) and a discharge temperature that falls as the store empties

detail: sensible storage

description: biomass or waste gasification to methanol: pretreatment, gasification, gas cleaning, reforming of hydrocarbons, water-gas shift and/or CO2 removal, methanol synthesis and distillation; feedstocks wood or by-product/waste streams (maize residue, forest residue, black liquor, rice straw)
forest-residue gasification to bio-methanol (VarmlandsMetanol, Sweden), proposed

detail: Chemrec Domsjo, bio-DME and methanol; capex per t of combined product
description: black liquor gasification at a pulp mill (Chemrec, Domsjo Fabriker, Sweden) co-producing bio-DME and bio-methanol for motor fuels; the gasifier replaces part of the recovery-boiler function
methanol from CO2 (atmospheric or flue-gas CO2) and hydrogen, typically electrolytic

detail: CRI Iceland, 1.6 kt/yr; the capex includes on-site electrolysis and CO2 recovery
description: renewable methanol from flue-gas CO2 and hydrogen from water electrolysis on geothermal and hydro power (Carbon Recycling International, Iceland)

detail: whole natural-gas methanol plant: reforming and synthesis
description: natural-gas-based methanol production (reforming and synthesis), the conventional route

detail: whole natural-gas methanol plant: reforming and synthesis
description: conventional natural-gas-based methanol plant (reforming and methanol synthesis), 1 Mt/yr, Bromberg & Cheng (2010) estimate - the fossil reference

multi-effect distillation thermal desalination: vapour from each vessel is condensed in the next and evaporates more feed at reduced pressure, at about 70 degC; heat and electricity; suits low-temperature heat (e.g. 70-90 degC geothermal)

multi-stage flash thermal desalination: saline feed water heated to 90-110 degC flashes to vapour in a series of stages at falling pressure; the vapour is condensed as fresh water and the brine rejected; heat and electricity, often in cogeneration with a power plant

detail: electrodialysis, brackish water; proxy
description: electrodialysis desalination: an electrical potential moves the salt ions through ion-selective membranes, leaving fresh water behind; mostly for brackish water because energy use rises with feed salinity; electricity only

detail: municipal seawater or brackish RO; proxy for industrial water treatment
description: reverse osmosis desalination: seawater or brackish water pressurised above the osmotic pressure by electric pumps so that fresh water passes a semi-permeable membrane and the salts stay behind; needs feed-water pre-treatment against fouling; electricity only

detail: Perth seawater RO plant; proxy
description: seawater reverse osmosis plant in Perth, Western Australia, buying electricity from a wind farm; designed to optimise energy use

catalytic dehydration of chemical-grade bio-ethanol to ethylene over an alumina or silica-alumina catalyst (endothermic); the ethylene is chemically identical to steam-cracker ethylene and feeds existing polyethylene, PVC, ethylene oxide and ethylene glycol plants

process: Pellet and torrefied pellet production (text p.4, p.7)

detail: MILENA indirect twin-bed, atmospheric
description: ECN MILENA indirect (allothermal) twin-bed gasifier at atmospheric pressure with OLGA oil-scrubber tar removal, deep S/Cl removal, pre-reformer, nickel-catalyst methanation and CO2/H2O removal, producing grid-quality bio-methane (bio-SNG) from wood. The gasification riser runs at 850 degC with steam; char, tar and dust burn in a bubbling-bed combustor heating the sand to about 925 degC. No air enters the gas, so the producer gas is nearly N2-free

detail: electrolyser, H2 shaft and EAF, per t liquid steel
description: hydrogen direct reduction (H-DR) steelmaking: an electrolyser supplies H2 to a Midrex-type reduction shaft operating at 800 degC; the DRI is compacted to hot-briquetted iron (HBI) and melted to liquid steel in an EAF. Surplus H2 is recycled and a condenser recovers heat to pre-heat the H2 feed. All process heat is electric. Model plant, not an operating one; system boundary excludes pelletising, casting and rolling
